newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top Deutsche economist derides talk of EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Top Deutsche economist derides talk of EMU delay.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG chief economist Norbert Walter said on Monday it was naive and destructive to talk of delaying Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Only children believe there is a realistic chance of an orderly one- or two-year delay," Walter told German radio.
Politicians who talked of postponing EMU beyond its planned January 1999 launch should know "how hard it is to agree a binding treaty among 15 independent nations," he said.
Walter said a less rigid approach to the Maastricht Treaty criteria was needed.

With regard to budget deficits, a sticking point for many countries including Germany, Walter said it would be important to take into account what the future outlook was, not just the numbers achieved in 1997.

Maastricht Treaty entry goals include one that countries cut their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product this year, a clause German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has rigorously interpreted as 3.0 percent.
"We must be sure that it (the deficit) will be lower in 1998 and 1999, only then is 3.2 or 3.3 percent acceptable for 1997," Walter said.
At the weekend, Commerzbank AG chairman Martin Kohlhaussen, the head of the German Banking Federation, also said he considered a deficit to GDP ratio of 3.2 or 3.3 percent to be acceptable.
